radio, The story of the Australian company who used 10 separate "neighborhoods" to represent the 10 different departments is an example of which visualization tool? |metaphor|brainstorming|prototype|sketching
radio, Stories, sketches, paper prototypes, and journey maps are all types of... |data analytics tools.|false positives.|false negatives.|visualization tools.
radio, 75% of our brain's sensory neurons are dedicated to... |processing visuals.|utilizing our imagination.|dissecting auditory cues.|comprehending abstract thoughts.
radio, Describing a baby as "a ten pound bundle of joy with a smile as bright as the sun" is an example of... |metaphor.|sketching.|false positive.|emptiness.

radio, Sketching within the Imagining phase can be a powerful medium to... |communicate ideas both visually and verbally.|communicate ideas verbally.|limit the types of responses you want to receive.|communicate ideas visually.
answers.definition: communicate ideas both visually and verbally.

answers.term: radio, In traditional R&D, we produce the "thing" as it is supposed to be, and then test. In the Imagining phase of DT, on the other hand, what do we do? |use the "thing" as a vehicle to a better conversation and to get better feedback|break down the "thing" into as many small parts as possible|analyze the "thing" as a quality assurance check|test the "thing" as fast as we can to arrive at a solution sooner
answers.definition: use the "thing" as a vehicle to a better conversation and to get better feedback

answers.term: radio, What has research shown us to be the least utilized Design Thinking tool? |specification of disconfirming data|surfacing assumptions behind ideas|experiments|using learning from experiments to iterate solutions

radio, Which of the following best exemplifies the mindset of a designer? |Antonio makes sure his hypotheses are DESCRIPTIVE.|Antonio uses hypothesis testing to explain what is, rather than what could be.|Antonio's work lends itself more to discovery than invention.|Antonio's work lends itself more to invention than discovery.
answers.definition: Antonio's work lends itself more to invention than discovery.

answers.term: radio, Esther is the lead designer on a project for a manufacturer of medical supplies, and her team has a solution in mind. Her teammates suggests that they should try for a better solution by taking a different approach, but Esther is hesitant to abandon what they already have. Of which Category 3 bias is this situation an example? |the Hypothesis Confirmation Bias|the Endowment Effect|the Availability Bias|the Planning Fallacy

radio, Carolyn is a member of a team of designers working on a branding project for a Fortune 500 company. The stress of the project has been intense, and after a few mistakes early on Carolyn wasn't sure if she would be able to remain on the team. But during testing, she really focuses and is able to use her learning from experiments to iterate some exciting solutions. This has given her the sense that she can recover from mistakes and make valuable contributions. Which of the following aspects of "becoming" related to learning in action best describes Carolyn's transformation? |She has become more empathetic|She has become more resilient|She has become more curious|She has become more collaborative

radio, It's important that we test our hypotheses in an organized and thoughful manner as we drive toward innovative solutions. Which of the following steps should we NOT include in our hypothesis-driven testing process? |Develop a set of competing hypotheses (prescriptive hypotheses)|Gather preliminary data to allow construction of descriptive hypotheses|Begin with an amiguous problem|Define the problem

radio, Anita is developing a customer feedback solution with a team of designers. The development process slowed nearly to a halt as they began testing, but things improved once Anita realized she had been too quick to dismiss ideas as "bad" instead of seeking out information that might prove her wrong. Which of the following mindset shifts related to learning in action best describes her experience? |moving from thinking like an investor to thinking like a creator|moving from seeking to test the concept in full for "proof" to treating ideas as hypotheses|moving from passing judgment to adopting investigative doubt that seeks out disconfirming data|moving from looking for "proof" to seeking directional guidance by triangulating data points
answers.definition: moving from passing judgment to adopting investigative doubt that seeks out disconfirming data

answers.term: radio, Amy is designing a prototype for a mobile app interface. She has conducted real-world experiments with a large group and gathered detailed feedback from potential consumers, but when she reveals an updated prototype to her project lead, the project lead says it seems like much of the most valuable feedback from testing isn't reflected in the update. Which of the following common error points is Amy most likely encountering? |addressing insights inadequately in our solutions|failing to gather user feedback|failing to iterate a new version of her prototype|translating small group solutions into a larger context and scale
answers.definition: addressing insights inadequately in our solutions

answers.term: radio, Shannon is the lead on a product design team for a sportswear company, and they have been conducting testing. Members of her team are openly complaining that their input isn't being considered and that Shannon is constantly overriding their opinions regarding the experimentation process. Which of the following difficult aspects of learning in action best describes the situation? |We want to be the decision maker|We think we need to maintain secrecy|Learning in action is often time-consuming|We can have a false sense that learning in action is optional
answers.definition: We want to be the decision maker

answers.term: radio, Eric is working on a water filtration system. He and his team are finally getting out in the field to test their system with a group of customers, and they're ready to carefully record the results. To which of the following steps from David Kolb's learning model does this most closely apply? |active experimentation|reflective observation|abstract conceptualization|concrete experience

radio, Claudia is designing an interface for an online shopping app with her team. They feel like they have gathered some strong ideas and gotten off to a good start, but they now want to build on their ideas and observations to create meaning and purpose within their design process that is both personal and shared. In which of the phases discussed in this course is Claudia's group currently working? |Alignment|Immersion|Sensemaking|Emergence

radio, Mary has just completed design thinking training and is ready to use what she learned on a new work project. What is an example of an impact she might expect to see on a personal level? |An increased sense of creative confidence and psychological safety|Increased solution quality and implementability for her project|Barriers to convincing her coworkers of the benefits of the DT process|As the only member of her team with DT training, the DT process may leave her feeling isolated from her team
answers.definition: An increased sense of creative confidence and psychological safety

answers.term: radio, Jessica is the manager of a product design team. As she conducts her research and investigation, she knows she needs to be wary of several natural human tendencies to achieve true immersion. Which of the following would be an example of these negative tendencies? |During an end-user interview, the interviewee says something about the product that Jessica finds completely ridiculous. She decides to dismiss the idea and moves the conversation in a different direction.|During the early stages of the design process, Jessica makes sure to avoid projecting her own preferences onto her coworkers.|Jessica uncovers some surprising information in an interview. Although there is no hard data to validate her discovery, she decides to pursue the idea further anyway.|After her first week on the project, Jessica isn't sure how she feels about her coworkers, but she is determined to get to know them better rather than avoiding them.
answers.definition: During an end-user interview, the interviewee says something about the product that Jessica finds completely ridiculous. She decides to dismiss the idea and moves the conversation in a different direction.

answers.term: radio, Which of the following should Jill avoid doing during the design thinking process? |Collecting accurate data|Using data from the past to predict the future|Looking for extreme users to help figure out what future is already happening|Confidently approaching open-ended problems without being able to see potential solutions
answers.definition: Using data from the past to predict the future

answers.term: radio, Martin is busy working on a solution for a beverage company, and he is approaching the sensemaking phase of design thinking. He has noticed while working on previous projects that sensemaking can change innovators and their mindsets. Why is that? |They are comfortable with ambiguity to discover deeper meanings.|They struggle to understand why users think and act as they do.|They don't reframe the definition of the problem and keep it simple.|They attempt to avoid conflict and try to get the "right" interpretation of data.
answers.definition: They are comfortable with ambiguity to discover deeper meanings.

answers.term: radio, John is the CEO for his firm and wants to lead an alignment session as part of a new initiative the firm is working on. He holds the meeting and is hesitant that any good will come from inviting a broad group of voices into the conversation, so he keeps the size small. Did he do something wrong? |Yes, John brought people in the room and let them meet without a formal agenda or structure to the conversation.|Yes, he attempted to over-control access and interaction with this meeting by limiting the group size.|Yes, he held the meeting. Coming from a senior leader this might drive fear in subordinates and they might not be comfortable sharing their true experiences and being vulnerable with their ideas.|No, he was trying to bring about the best ideas by carefully designing and managing the conversation.
answers.definition: Yes, he attempted to over-control access and interaction with this meeting by limiting the group size.

answers.term: radio, Eliza is attempting a new effective dialogue technique for her team. She creates dialogue around the positive elements of an issue and involves asking questions that improve the capability to reach its positive potential. What term refers to this style of effective dialogue? |Future Search|Appreciative Inquiry|World Cafe|Democratic Dialogue

radio, Which of the following best describes what Kathryn Schultz calls "investigative doubt?" |the attitude of doubt fueled by cynicism rather than curiosity|the attitude of doubt fueled by curiosity rather than cynicism|the "allure of certainty"|the emotional benefits of living with certainty
answers.definition: the attitude of doubt fueled by curiosity rather than cynicism

answers.term: radio, Which of the following best exemplifies the mindset of a scientist? |Anna's work lends itself more to discovery than invention.|Anna makes sure her hypotheses are PRESCRIPTIVE.|Anna uses hypothesis testing to explain what could be, rather than what is.|Anna's work lends itself more to invention than discovery.
answers.definition: Anna's work lends itself more to discovery than invention.

answers.term: radio, David is the lead designer on a project for a prominent car manufacturer. One of the members of his team has brought him an idea that the others seem very excited about. David has a hard time envisioning the idea, so he tells the team he's going to go with a more familiar approach. Of which Category 3 bias is this situation an example? |the Planning Fallacy|the Hypothesis Confirmation Bias|the Endowment Effect|the Availability Bias

radio, Steve is a member of a team of designers working on a branding project for a Fortune 500 company. He has enjoyed the process overall, but early on he found himself a little overwhelmed by the pace of changes that occured as the team prepared to test their prototypes with consumers. Once he changes some habits and reorients his focus to better fit the developments of the project, he is able to make some key contributions during the testing process. Which of following aspects of "becoming" related to learning in action best describes Steve's transformation? |He has become more confident|He has become more empathetic|He has become more curious|He has become more adaptive

radio, It's important that we test our hypotheses in an organized and thoughful manner as we drive toward innovative solutions. Which of the following steps should we include in our hypothesis-driven testing process? |Gather preliminary data to allow construction of prescriptive hypotheses|Define the problem|Set aside anomolies and disconcerting data|Begin with an ambiguous problem

radio, Jerome is developing an inventory management solution with a team of designers. The development process had a bumpy start, but as they moved through testing their solutions with managers in the field, Jerome noticed that admitting some of his personal mistakes - which he found hard to do earlier - allowed him and his team to correct errors and improve their testing. Which of the following mindset shifts related to learning in action best describes his experience? |moving from seeking to test the concept in full for "proof" to treating ideas as hypotheses|moving from passing judgment to adopting investigative doubt|going from needing to be right to being willing to be wrong|moving from looking for "proof" to seeking directional guidance by triangulating data points
answers.definition: going from needing to be right to being willing to be wrong

answers.term: radio, Mark decided to forego real-world experimentation while designing a project for his client. He conducted many user interviews during the design process, but there are a number of error reports coming in during the initial deployment of the solution. Which of the following common error points is Mark most likely encountering? |translating small group solutions into a larger context and scale|failing to gather user feedback|misinterpreting interview data when mining for insights|addressing insights inadequately in solutions
answers.definition: misinterpreting interview data when mining for insights

answers.term: radio, Which of the following best describes the process of presencing? |the whole becoming greater than the sum of its parts|selecting the least worst solution to which everyone will agree|requisite variety|letting go of biases, assumptions and, ownership of ideas so we can "let come" new concepts
answers.definition: letting go of biases, assumptions and, ownership of ideas so we can "let come" new concepts

answers.term: radio, Leaving room for others to create what COULD BE instead of being told what WILL BE is an example of the power of... |complex adaptive systems.|emptiness.|presencing.|emergent diversity.

radio, Which of the following best describes the "boss effect?" |It has no effect on the Emergence experience.|It elevates the Emergence experience.|It enhances the Emergence experience.|It detracts from the Emergence experience.
answers.definition: It detracts from the Emergence experience.

answers.term: radio, The most productive strategy when pairing business leaders and designers together in teams suggests that... |team members should wait for the highest-level person in the room to pronounce a solution.|business leaders should attempt to engage in visualization techniques alongside designers.|each department should focus only on what they do best.|designers should do the visualizing and business leaders should do the enterprise work.
answers.definition: business leaders should attempt to engage in visualization techniques alongside designers.

answers.term: radio, We know that if you ask people in a focus group if they will buy a product, 50% will say yes but will never actually buy it. This is what kind of response? |Chaos theory|False positive|False negative|Metaphor

radio, A member of your design team suggested a promising idea at the beginning of your project. With time, however, the idea became less feasible. Despite the rest of the team being ready to move on and test a new hypothesis, the original team member struggles to let go of their initial idea. This is an example of: |A Category 3 bias|A Category 2 bias|A Category 1 bias|Selective perception

radio, John has joined a team that is developing a branding solution for a client, and he wants to use this opportunity to become a better designer and innovator. At what point has John experienced the culmination of DT methodology? |Once he can fully map out his customers' experience with a product|Once he has achieved full proficiency of the technical elements of design|Only once he becomes so accustomed to using the tools above that he becomes immersed in understanding his stakeholders' experience|When he has mastered the use of ethnographic tools
answers.definition: Only once he becomes so accustomed to using the tools above that he becomes immersed in understanding his stakeholders' experience

answers.term: radio, Which of the following DOES NOT aid our capacity to understand the needs of others? |Mirror neurons|The part of the limbic system that triggers fear|Affective empathy|The virtuous cycle
answers.definition: The part of the limbic system that triggers fear

answers.term: radio, Danny wants to use DT to gain a better understanding of his stakeholders. Which of the following should he prioritize last according to DT core practices? |Using surveys to gather quantitative data on customer behavior|Using ethnographic tools to identify insights|Developing a deeper understanding of the stakeholders' context|Conducting interviews to learn about the details of people's lives and unmet needs
answers.definition: Using surveys to gather quantitative data on customer behavior

answers.term: radio, Which of the following problems would NOT be best-served by hypothesis-driven thinking? |Understanding why a patient's journey from a provider room to the lab is taking longer than expected|Figuring out how to best reduce a cafeteria's carbon footprint|Creating financial projections for the upcoming year|Prototyping a new product
answers.definition: Creating financial projections for the upcoming year

answers.term: radio, Maggie is great at cognitive empathy, but struggles with affective empathy. Which of the following is Maggie likely to be good at handling? |Maggie is tasked with preparing for a negotiation where it will be important to understand her opponent's way of thinking.|As a brand manager, Maggie needs to understand how her customers make emotional connections with her brand.|Maggie's boss asks her for advice about what she feels the emotional reaction of her coworkers will be in response to a controversial work policy.|Maggie gets a call from her best friend Bonnie whose dog just died. Bonnie asks her to come over because she needs a friend.
answers.definition: Maggie is tasked with preparing for a negotiation where it will be important to understand her opponent's way of thinking.

answers.term: radio, Heather is a project lead working for a sporting goods company. She has formed a group, and is striving to achieve alignment for an upcoming project. What is a critical FIRST step for her that cannot be overlooked? |Making sure to form a large group of people in order to bring about the best ideas|Designing and developing user stories and journey maps for the people they are designing for|Setting some structure to the alignment meeting and making sure to have someone take notes|Understanding and aligning on the definition of the problem and the needs for whom they are designing for
answers.definition: Understanding and aligning on the definition of the problem and the needs for whom they are designing for

answers.term: radio, Edmi has a revolutionary idea that she believes will help improve the speed at which clinics can operate, leaving people sitting in the wait room less, getting what they need, and leaving satisfied from their visit. Instead of going through the key process of sensemaking alone, she plans to involve a team of other people. Why is this important? |Each person sharing their ideas allows for others to correct your thinking.|It allows each individual to solidify their own ideas against other ideas.|Sensemaking in a team leaves less room for error as there are more people to work with.|She can uncover new insights and dig deeper than one ever could have individually.
answers.definition: She can uncover new insights and dig deeper than one ever could have individually.

answers.term: radio, Michelle wants to create an environment for his team to practice design thinking and alignment without making anyone feel uncomfortable. She writes out why dialogue and the emphasis on dialogue is important in these meetings in order to get alignment. Which of these is NOT an emphasis of dialogue? |inclusivity and an openness to being individually changed by the conversation|intention to act as a collective|willingness to share honestly and listen with an open mind|creating a formal process through negotiation
answers.definition: creating a formal process through negotiation

answers.term: radio, Sarah is designing a new product for a clothing company, and she is planning to hold a sensemaking discussion with her team. While she is holding the session, she wants to make sure their process addresses the right audience. What should be her and her team's target audience for their product? |A general audience - it's not necessary to refine the audience just yet|The people in the middle of the bell curve and the outliers at each extreme|The majority of people - those who fall in the middle of the bell curve|The outliers at the extreme ends of the curve whose needs may be radically different from the norm
answers.definition: The people in the middle of the bell curve and the outliers at each extreme

answers.term: radio, The goal of the Emergence stage is to... |allow one individual to take control of the process.|help shift innovators from a state of individualized, isolated problem-solving to a collective state of possibility-thinking.|stage a path to return to the Immersion phase.|narrow down topics of conversation.
answers.definition: help shift innovators from a state of individualized, isolated problem-solving to a collective state of possibility-thinking.

answers.term: radio, Why does giving groups a lit-up light bulb (a symbol for the "Aha!" moment) yield greater creative output than those who did not receive such a stimulus? |The group who received the light bulb was able to harness the energy of the bulb to power their parietal lobe.|Words are more capable of sparking creativity than visuals.|Visual metaphors create a shortcut around normal language processes that aim straight for how we think and feel.|Visual metaphors block our frontal cortex from triggering commands to form images.
answers.definition: Visual metaphors create a shortcut around normal language processes that aim straight for how we think and feel.

answers.term: radio, What does Michael Lissack mean when he explains how "the storyteller carves out a canyon for the listener to supply a river of meaning to run through it?" |Listeners can hear a story, interpret their own meaning and, as a result, transform their beliefs and behaviors in a way that resonates with them.|In order for storytellers to be successful, they must repeat their stories over a long period of time to achieve significant meaning.|It is more effective to sketch the message you are attempting to convey than tell it via word of mouth.|Stories are powerful visualization tools because everyone gleans the same information from the same story.
answers.definition: Listeners can hear a story, interpret their own meaning and, as a result, transform their beliefs and behaviors in a way that resonates with them.

answers.term: radio, Instead of viewing prototypes as "dress rehearsals" for a finished product, we should view them as... |a return to the Immersion phase.|provocations to engage others in rich conversation.|the finished product.|noncritical vehicles of our assumptions.
answers.definition: provocations to engage others in rich conversation.

answers.term: radio, The barriers to learning in the Testing phase are deeply grounded in one of the most basic human desires to... |be right.|attribute success to someone else.|work alone.|question authority.

radio, Greg is working on a product design for a lawncare company, and they are currently conducting testing. Throughout the process, he is constantly fixating on small details and noting minor imperfections with experiments. This is making it hard to move forward, and his teammates are becoming frustated with the process. Which of the following difficult aspects of learning in action best describes Greg's situation? |We think we need to maintain secrecy|He's seeking perfection|Everyone wants to be the decision maker|We can have a false sense that learning in action is optional

radio, Natasha is working toward experimentation on a road safety solution. She thinks back on specific times from her past in which she worked on public safety projects, and makes notes about how they might apply to her current project. To which of the following steps from David Kolb's learning model does this action most closely apply? |reflective obersvation|concrete experience|active experimentation|abstract conceptualization

radio, You are introducing value chain analysis to your team. You explain that value chain analysis can be considered the "organizational perspective" version of a different Design Thinking tool. Which tool is it? |Journey map|Design brief|Persona matrix|Prototype

radio, A senior director has invited you to a meeting to discuss the organizational challenge that you and your team are tackling using Design Thinking. The director asks you to describe value chain analysis as used in Design Thinking. Which of the following is your best response? |The method to test key assumptions in four areas: value, execution, scale, and sustainability (including defensibility)|The specific tools that the team will use throughout the Design Thinking questions of "What Is," "What If," "What Wows," and "What Works"|A structured approach to working with a large mass of research data and converging on a set of design insights|The study of an organization's interaction with partners to produce, market, distribute, and support its offerings
answers.definition: The study of an organization's interaction with partners to produce, market, distribute, and support its offerings

answers.term: radio, Your team is getting ready to tackle a new organizational challenge using the Design Thinking process. When is the first, best time to conduct an end-to-end value chain analysis? |Immediately before the first learning launch|During concept development|Right after establishing design criteria|During the exploration phase

radio, Your team is eager to focus on innovation possibilities - and you introduce value chain analysis. This seems like a waste of time to them. They could be creating solutions! A team member yawns and asks you to explain the benefit of value chain analysis. Which of the following is your best response? |It helps ensure that our solution will be sustainable for the organization in the long term.|It helps ensure that our solution will support the status quo (current, existing situation).|It helps ensure that our solution will be consistent with the industry's dominant logic.|It helps ensure that our solution will be exclusively customer focused, at whatever cost to our partners.
answers.definition: It helps ensure that our solution will be sustainable for the organization in the long term.

answers.term: radio, You and your team are ready to draw the value chain for your organization. What is your first best step? |Identify the core strategic capabilities needed.|Work backwards from the end user.|Evaluate the bargaining power of each player.|Analyze the competitive environment.
answers.definition: Work backwards from the end user.

answers.term: radio, An executive in your organization is interested in learning more about the Design Thinking tool: value chain analysis. The executive asks you what types of opportunities are appropriate for value chain analysis. Which of the following is your best response? |Strategic industry-wide opportunities|Individual and project-team opportunities|Multiple levels, from specific opportunities to broader situations|Tactical department-level opportunities
answers.definition: Multiple levels, from specific opportunities to broader situations

answers.term: radio, You and your team are at the point in the Design Thinking process where you are ready to start generating ideas. You suggest that the team first take time to revisit the value chain analysis that they created earlier. Why? |Spot inefficiencies that are ripe for rearrangement, perhaps by shifting boundaries in the chain.|Acknowledge reality and work within the current competitive environment.|Innovate exclusively within the organization's established market activities and capabilities.|Ensure that the team is clear on existing boundaries to protect the status quo (current situation).
answers.definition: Spot inefficiencies that are ripe for rearrangement, perhaps by shifting boundaries in the chain.

answers.term: radio, Your team is drawing your organization's existing value chain. As the team works, you suggest that they also spend time analyzing and understanding the dynamics involved in the chain. Which of the following is a benefit of understanding these dynamics as you make your innovation decisions? |The ability to determine where to place innovation resources|The ability to set aside our organization's vulnerabilities|The ability to gain and maintain control of the entire value chain|The ability to disregard situations that are out of our control
answers.definition: The ability to determine where to place innovation resources

answers.term: radio, As Jeanne Liedtka explains in our video, the learning that you gain from value chain analysis can support your work as a leader. You can use value chain analysis to help you gain strategic new insights into your own innovation challenges and opportunities. She recommends three categories to help you translate value chain analysis findings into your personal action plan. What are the three categories? |Keep, lose, create|Identify, discuss, prioritize|Listen, analyze, resolve|Publicize, sell, negotiate

radio, Another Design Thinking team has requested your expertise! They are tackling a challenge related to new product development. Their team is constructing a value chain for this innovation challenge. The team knows that they should include a fundamental value proposition in their value chain drawing - but they are not sure whose perspective it should represent. Which of the following is your best answer? |The suppliers who will provide components|The director who will lead the manufacturing effort|The executive board who will approve product funding|The customer who will use the product
answers.definition: The customer who will use the product

answers.term: radio, Which of the following is NOT an example of an outcome DT can achieve for an organization? |Powerful personal level impacts|Ensuring the desired insights to a problem|Creating conditions for higher order ideas to emerge during stakeholder conversations|Relationship building impacts from use of DT that is related to network capability and resource use
answers.definition: Ensuring the desired insights to a problem

answers.term: radio, Which of the following is an example of a Category 1 bias? |Say/Do Gap|Project Bias|Planning Fallacy|Response Bias

radio, What is the culmination of DT's social technology? |Mastery of design tools such as ethnography and prototyping|An innovator's personal transformation through the process of doing-experiencing-becoming|Helping innovators understand their customer's journey|Delivering on an organization's innovation wish list
answers.definition: An innovator's personal transformation through the process of doing-experiencing-becoming

answers.term: radio, Which of the following is NOT one of the five core practices of design thinking? |Ensure requisite variety|Offer a structured and facilitated process|Create multiple solutions and make them tangible and testable|Form diverse teams
radio, Which of the following is an example of a Category 3 bias? |Projection Bias|Say/Do Gap|Endowment Effect|Response Bias

radio, Which of the following is illustrative of a positive mindset shift when it comes to Immersion? |You remain certain about the accuracy of our own perspective.|You accept the definition of the problem you have been given.|You become more critical of the obvious definition and begin to treat it as a hypothesis that needs testing.|You remain egocentric.
answers.definition: You become more critical of the obvious definition and begin to treat it as a hypothesis that needs testing.

answers.term: radio, Which of the following best describes an egocentric empahty bias? |It doesn't really affect our experience of immersion.|It's a bias wherein we consistently under-estimate the similarity between what we value and what others value.|It's a bias wherein we consistently over-estimate the similarity between what we value and what others value.|It's an example of a Category 3 bias.
answers.definition: It's a bias wherein we consistently over-estimate the similarity between what we value and what others value.

answers.term: radio, Which of the following best describes the role of mirror neurons in the brain? |Some scientists believe they are the biological root of empathy.|They are irrelevant when discussing where human empathy comes from.|They are irrelevant to the role of Immersion in DT.|They inhibit our ability to express empahty.
answers.definition: Some scientists believe they are the biological root of empathy.

answers.term: radio, Which of the following are common challenges of immersion that can show up for us personally as we navigate the Design process? |We listen to judge rather than to understand.|We listen to understand rather than to judge.|Most of us embrace stepping into the unknown.|We tend to listen through the solutions we already have in mind.
answers.definition: We listen to judge rather than to understand.

answers.term: radio, Which of the following types of empathy should Maggie work to develop during the DT process? |Emotional Empathy|Cognitive Empathy|Both Cognitive and Affective Empathy|Affective Empathy

radio, Which of the following is NOT a reason why Design Thinking, specifically sensemaking, is better conducted in teams/groups? |It is difficult to see our own biases and blinders.|Conflict and confrontation should be avoided to move the project forward.|Provocation from others helps to surface unarticulated beliefs and assumptions.|Other people help to interrupt our habitual ways to find deeper insights.
answers.definition: Conflict and confrontation should be avoided to move the project forward.

answers.term: radio, Why does sensemaking set up evidence-based idea generation? |It promotes diligence in establishing solid evidence about a group of people's needs.|Each individual is able to contribute the ideas inside their head.|It helps to understand what is most important to the group.|Exploring what is known brings further knowledge about the group of people and their needs.
answers.definition: It promotes diligence in establishing solid evidence about a group of people's needs.

answers.term: radio, What is the #1 rule for sensemaking? |Form a team early and stick with the same people.|Other people help to uncover deeper insights and interrupt our habitual ways.|Brainstorm in a very structured manner in order to bring about the best ideas.|There are no rules. It's a black box or a puzzle.
answers.definition: There are no rules. It's a black box or a puzzle.

answers.term: radio, Design criteria - the specific criteria for future designs - play a pivotal role in Design Thinking through... |discovering the boundaries of our ideas and how far to one extreme they should go.|encouraging more productive idea generation by giving stakeholders the opportunity to determine what is important before they start generating ideas.|allowing solutions to be changed throughout the process when new ideas are developed during testing|setting standards that aren't set in stone in order to have fluidity in the design
answers.definition: encouraging more productive idea generation by giving stakeholders the opportunity to determine what is important before they start generating ideas.

answers.term: radio, Bên Kiểm soát dữ liệu cá nhân có quyền và trách nhiệm như thế nào? |Chỉ thực hiện xử lý dữ liệu theo hợp đồng hoặc thỏa thuận.|Không quyết định mục đích, mà chỉ thực hiện theo chỉ thị của Bên Kiểm soát dữ liệu.|Có quyền và trách nhiệm cao nhất trong việc định hướng, kiểm soát việc sử dụng dữ liệu.|Vai trò phát sinh khi có sự chia sẻ, chuyển giao dữ liệu cho mục đích khác ngoài hoạt động xử lý ban đầu.
answers.definition: Có quyền và trách nhiệm cao nhất trong việc định hướng, kiểm soát việc sử dụng dữ liệu.

answers.term: radio, Ví dụ nào sau đây thể hiện vai trò của Bên Xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân? |Một công ty thương mại điện tử quyết định thu thập tên, địa chỉ, lịch sử mua hàng của khách hàng để gửi quảng cáo.|Một bệnh viện quyết định lưu trữ hồ sơ bệnh án điện tử để phục vụ khám chữa bệnh.|Một công ty cung cấp dịch vụ điện toán đám mây lưu trữ dữ liệu khách hàng cho một ngân hàng.|Một doanh nghiệp tự xây dựng và vận hành hệ thống quản lý nhân sự, thu thập và xử lý thông tin nhân viên của mình.
answers.definition: Một công ty cung cấp dịch vụ điện toán đám mây lưu trữ dữ liệu khách hàng cho một ngân hàng.

answers.term: radio, Cơ quan nào sau đây là cơ quan chuyên trách bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân? |Bộ Khoa học và Công nghệ.|Bộ Thông tin và Truyền thông.|Bộ Công an (Cục An ninh mạng và phòng, chống tội phạm sử dụng công nghệ cao - A05).|Ủy ban nhân dân các tỉnh, thành phố trực thuộc Trung ương.
answers.definition: Bộ Công an (Cục An ninh mạng và phòng, chống tội phạm sử dụng công nghệ cao - A05).

answers.term: radio, Quyền nào sau đây không phải là quyền của Chủ thể dữ liệu? |Quyền được biết: Chủ thể dữ liệu được biết về hoạt động xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân của mình.|Quyền truy cập: Chủ thể dữ liệu được truy cập để xem, chỉnh sửa dữ liệu cá nhân của mình.|Quyền rút lại sự đồng ý: Chủ thể dữ liệu được quyền rút lại sự đồng ý bất cứ lúc nào.|Quyền tùy ý sử dụng dữ liệu cá nhân của người khác mà không cần sự cho phép.
answers.definition: Quyền tùy ý sử dụng dữ liệu cá nhân của người khác mà không cần sự cho phép.

answers.term: radio, Nghĩa vụ nào sau đây không phải là nghĩa vụ của Chủ thể dữ liệu? |Tự bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân của mình: Cảnh giác, sử dụng các biện pháp bảo mật.|Cung cấp dữ liệu cá nhân đầy đủ, chính xác: Đảm bảo thông tin đúng sự thật.|Tham gia tuyên truyền, phổ biến kỹ năng bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân: Chung tay xây dựng cộng đồng an toàn thông tin.|Khai thác, sử dụng trái phép dữ liệu cá nhân của người khác.
answers.definition: Khai thác, sử dụng trái phép dữ liệu cá nhân của người khác.

answers.term: radio, Trách nhiệm chính của Bên Xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân là gì? |Quyết định mục đích và phương tiện xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân.|Chuyển giao dữ liệu cá nhân ra nước ngoài.|Chỉ nhận dữ liệu cá nhân và xử lý theo hợp đồng hoặc thỏa thuận với Bên Kiểm soát dữ liệu cá nhân.|Xây dựng và ban hành quy định nội bộ về bảo vệ dữ liệu.
answers.definition: Chỉ nhận dữ liệu cá nhân và xử lý theo hợp đồng hoặc thỏa thuận với Bên Kiểm soát dữ liệu cá nhân.

answers.term: radio, Hành vi nào sau đây bị nghiêm cấm trong hoạt động bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân? |Xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân theo quy định của pháp luật.|Xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân để chống lại Nhà nước Cộng hòa xã hội chủ nghĩa Việt Nam.|Áp dụng các biện pháp bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân.|Không cản trở hoạt động bảo vệ dữ liệu cá nhân của cơ quan có thẩm quyền.

answers.term: radio, Nguyên tắc nào sau đây không phải là điều kiện hợp pháp để thu thập và xử lý dữ liệu cá nhân? |Hợp pháp, công bằng, minh bạch: Xử lý dữ liệu phải có căn cứ pháp luật và rõ ràng.|Hạn chế theo mục đích: Chỉ xử lý dữ liệu cho các mục đích đã được xác định, công bố.|Tối thiểu hóa dữ liệu: Chỉ thu thập dữ liệu cần thiết cho mục đích.|Tùy ý sử dụng dữ liệu không giới hạn thời gian.

answers.definition: Để bảo vệ tính mạng, sức khỏe của chủ thể dữ liệu hoặc người khác trong trường hợp khẩn cấp.

answers.term: radio, Read the following statements from a discussion on what we can personally do to combat population growth. - "We need to be more mindful of our consumption of natural resources, such as taking shorter showers." - "Do think that really helps? That seems like a drop in the bucket. If I take a shorter shower, it is not going to affect the people in India." - "I agree. Even if you do these things, not everyone will. I think what we need to do is to make other people aware of the problem instead of just working on yourself." - "I personally think that population growth, environmental issues, and poverty are all related to education. Education is the solution to these problems. Education will help people make better decisions that will impact the negative effect people have on the earth and how we get along with each other." What is the best synthesizing statement below for the the ideas above? |Although being mindful of our personal usage of natural resources is a good thing to do, it will not really make much of an impact on population growth. We need to educate and make people aware of the problem.|Taking shorter showers will not help slow down population growth.|Some ways to preserve our natural resources are to take shorter showers and to recycle your bottles and cans.
answers.definition: Although being mindful of our personal usage of natural resources is a good thing to do, it will not really make much of an impact on population growth. We need to educate and make people aware of the problem.

undefined, Empathy is the ability to recognize emotions and to share perspectives with others. It is one of the five key components of emotional intelligence, and it helps to build trust and strengthen relationships. In this assignment, you will reflect on how you can practice and build empathy in your daily life. Write a response (300-400 words) addressing the following: Three Stages of Empathy: Reflect on a recent interaction (at work, school, or personal life). How could you have applied cognitive empathy, emotional empathy, and compassionate empathy? Practicing Empathy: Which empathy practices (e.g., "walking in their shoes," assuming positive intent, listening better) would have helped you understand the other person more fully? Application in Teams: How can empathy improve collaboration, performance, or well-being in your team or organization? Personal Growth: What specific step will you take this week to strengthen your empathy skills? Your response will be reviewed by Coursera's AI-assisted evaluation, which will provide feedback on how well you applied course concepts and reflected on personal practice. |
answers.definition: Recently, I had a conversation with a colleague who seemed frustrated about a project deadline. Reflecting on the interaction, I realize I could have applied the three stages of empathy more effectively. First, cognitive empathy would have helped me step into their perspective and recognize the pressure they were feeling, rather than focusing only on my own workload. Second, emotional empathy would have allowed me to connect with their stress on a human level by acknowledging their feelings and validating that the situation was difficult. Finally, compassionate empathy would have prompted me to not only understand and feel with them, but also to offer concrete support—such as helping prioritize tasks or sharing part of the responsibility. In practicing empathy, two specific strategies stand out. The first is listening more intentionally—giving my colleague full attention instead of thinking about how I would respond. The second is assuming positive intent, which means reminding myself that their frustration was not directed at me personally but was a natural reaction to a challenging situation. If I had practiced these, I would have understood their perspective more fully and responded with patience instead of defensiveness. Applying empathy within teams has clear benefits. When team members feel heard and understood, it builds trust and psychological safety, making it easier for people to share ideas openly. This not only improves collaboration and creativity but also reduces conflict and stress. Empathy also enhances performance because individuals are more motivated when they feel supported, and it strengthens well-being by creating a culture where people know their emotions matter. This week, I plan to take one specific step to strengthen my empathy skills: practicing active listening in every conversation. Instead of jumping to problem-solving or defending my point of view, I will focus on paraphrasing what the other person says and checking my understanding. By doing this consistently, I can train myself to slow down, connect more deeply, and respond with greater empathy.

answers.term: undefined, In this assignment, you'll reflect on what you learned in this module and how you can apply it in your personal and professional life. Write a short response (250-400 words) that addresses the following questions: What did you take away from the self-regulation module and the exercises? What did you learn about yourself and others? What did you learn about your cognitive distortions and how thoughts affect feelings? How will you use the pause technique? How will you manage stress moving forward? Please be thoughtful and honest in your reflection. Your responses will be reviewed by Coursera's AI-assisted evaluation, which will provide you with personalized feedback. |
answers.definition: In this module on self-regulation, one of my main takeaways was recognizing how much my thoughts directly influence my emotions and behaviors. The exercises helped me slow down and observe patterns I normally overlook. For example, I realized that when I experience setbacks, I often fall into “all-or-nothing” thinking, assuming that one mistake means total failure. By identifying these cognitive distortions, I gained a clearer understanding that my emotions are not always accurate reflections of reality but rather shaped by the way I interpret situations. Through this process, I also learned more about myself and others. I noticed that when I am stressed, I tend to withdraw, while others may become more reactive or outspoken. Recognizing these differences has made me more empathetic and patient. Instead of assuming people are being “difficult,” I now see that they may simply have different coping styles. This perspective helps me approach personal and professional relationships with more understanding. The module highlighted the importance of the pause technique, which I found especially useful. Taking a brief pause before reacting gives me space to choose a more thoughtful response rather than letting automatic emotions control me. For example, if I receive critical feedback at work, instead of feeling defensive right away, I can pause, breathe, and remind myself that feedback is an opportunity to learn. Moving forward, I plan to manage stress by combining the pause technique with healthier routines. This includes scheduling short breaks during the day, practicing mindfulness, and reframing negative self-talk into more balanced perspectives. By applying these tools, I feel more equipped to handle challenges calmly and to maintain better emotional balance both in my professional life and in personal relationships.

answers.definition: A. 6Ws (Problem Identification, ~160 words) The problem I face is the delay in updating our project documentation for the marketing campaign launch. Who: I am responsible for drafting and updating the content, while my manager reviews it. What: Several documents, including the campaign brief and social media schedule, are outdated, causing confusion among team members. When: The issue arises during weekly planning sessions, as tasks rely on the most recent version of the documents. Where: This occurs in our shared Google Drive workspace, where multiple team members edit and rely on the files. Why: The updates are often postponed because I prioritize urgent tasks, and no fixed routine exists for documentation. How: The lack of clear ownership and a set schedule means the documents lag behind actual project progress, which creates misalignment in deadlines and task assignments. B. My Role (~95 words) My role is to draft, update, and share these documents on time. I help by ensuring the content is accurate and accessible, but I also hinder the process when I delay updates in favor of “urgent” tasks. My constraints include balancing competing deadlines and limited review availability from my manager. I assume that if I adopt a routine for updates, the team will use the documents consistently. My responsibility is to streamline this process within four weeks by managing my own time and setting clear checkpoints. C. Goal-Oriented Question How might I update and share the campaign brief and schedule for my team so that all members work from accurate, current documents by the end of this month?

answers.definition: A. Reframed Goal-Oriented Question How might I update and share the campaign brief and schedule for my team so that all members work from accurate, current documents by the end of this month? B. Brainstorm List Set a fixed weekly time block to update documents. Use calendar reminders to signal update deadlines. Automate document versioning using Google Drive add-ons. Assign a backup person to review and update if I’m unavailable. Create a checklist for campaign updates. Hold a short weekly sync meeting to confirm document accuracy. Track edits with version history and highlight changes. Request my manager to review documents on a fixed schedule. C. Three Chosen Options Set a fixed weekly time block with calendar reminders. Create a checklist for campaign updates. Hold a short weekly sync meeting to confirm document accuracy. D. Advantages and Disadvantages (~160 words) The first option, setting a fixed weekly time block with reminders, ensures consistency and makes documentation updates part of my regular workflow. Its advantage is predictability, but a disadvantage is that urgent tasks could still interfere, and I’ll need discipline to protect this time. The second option, creating a checklist, offers clarity and reduces the chance of missing details in the updates. Its main advantage is simplicity—anyone can follow the list. The disadvantage is that a checklist alone doesn’t enforce accountability; I could still postpone updates if not motivated. The third option, holding a short weekly sync meeting, brings team accountability since everyone confirms accuracy together. The advantage is collective responsibility and immediate feedback, but the disadvantage is time cost—it adds another meeting to already busy schedules, which may face resistance.

Hearing phrases like “we don’t have time for that” or seeing teammates overlook updated documents can make me feel that my work isn’t valued. Potential Triggering Responses A teammate might say the weekly sync meeting is a “waste of time.” My manager might push back, arguing that updates should be flexible rather than scheduled. C. Recommendation (2–3 sentences) My proposed solution is to block a fixed weekly time to update documents, supported by a simple checklist. This approach ensures consistency, keeps the workload manageable, and avoids adding extra meetings to the team’s schedule. It balances structure with efficiency and provides a clear system for keeping documents accurate. D. Feedback Strategy (~100 words) If I receive critical feedback on this recommendation, I will first listen carefully without interrupting and make sure I understand the concerns fully. Instead of reacting defensively, I will ask clarifying questions to uncover whether the concern is about workload, practicality, or team engagement. Then, I would acknowledge the feedback and suggest a compromise, such as starting with a trial period or combining my plan with another idea. answers.definition: After scoring myself on the feedback skills assessment, I landed in the “moderate” range. I wasn’t entirely surprised by the results because I know I give feedback regularly, but I also recognize that I don’t always deliver it as clearly or constructively as I could. The score confirmed what I already sensed: I’m competent but still have room to grow. The main areas I need to improve are being more specific and timely with my feedback, and making sure I balance constructive criticism with acknowledgment of strengths. At times, I delay giving feedback because I worry about how the other person will react, and when I finally share it, the message may come across less impactful or harder to act on. To strengthen my feedback skills, one strategy I plan to try is using the SBI model (Situation–Behavior–Impact) to make feedback concrete and focused on observable actions rather than personal traits. Another strategy is to ask for feedback more frequently myself, so I can model openness and create a two-way dialogue. Both approaches should help me build confidence and improve the way feedback is exchanged in my professional and personal relationships.

answers.definition: Effective Networking Habits Two networking habits I already practice are showing authenticity and being generous. Two habits I want to improve are taking initiative and following up. answers.term: undefined, You've just explored how adaptability and resilience can be cultivated through conscious planning, flexible thinking, and self-awareness. Now, you will design your own personal action plan. This assignment builds on the discussion prompt you completed with peers. Reflect carefully and respond to the prompts below. Coursera Coach will provide AI-powered feedback to help you refine your plan and identify next steps for growth. Control, Influence, Accept (CIA Framework): List 3-5 aspects of your personal or professional life. Place each on the continuum of Control - Influence - Accept. Why did you place them there? Adaptive and Resilient Behaviors: Choose at least one adaptive behavior and one resilient behavior you want to strengthen (examples provided in the discussion). How will you practice them? Managing SCARF Triggers: Identify one situation where you've experienced a SCARF trigger (Status, Certainty, Autonomy, Relatedness, Fairness). How could you manage that trigger differently in the future? Flexible Planning in a VUCA World: Provide one example of how you could plan multiple possible outcomes for a challenge at work or school. How does this approach help you stay adaptable? Small Goals & Measuring Progress: Set 1-2 small, measurable goals for cultivating adaptability or resilience. How will you track your progress? |
answers.definition: A. Control – Influence – Accept (3–5 aspects) My daily schedule & time-blocking — Control. I can decide my calendar, set routines, and protect focus blocks. Team documentation and update process — Influence. I can propose and run the process, but it requires teammates’ buy-in. Project roadmap and feature priorities set by leadership — Accept. Decisions come from leaders; I adapt and communicate impacts. My professional skill growth (learning new tools) — Control. I choose learning time, courses, and practice projects. Team morale and collaboration norms — Influence. I can model behaviors and suggest rituals (e.g., retros), but the whole team shapes culture. B. Adaptive & Resilient behaviors (what to strengthen + how) Adaptive behavior: Flexible planning & rapid experiments. Practice: each week create a Plan A/B for one task (small experiment), run the cheaper option first, record results in a 10-minute decision log. Resilient behavior: Emotion regulation (pause technique) and quick recovery routines. Practice: before responding in tense moments, do a 60-second pause (breath + label emotion), then choose response; follow up stressful days with a 20-minute reset (walk or short mindfulness). C. Managing a SCARF trigger Trigger experienced: Autonomy — I felt frustrated when tasks were assigned without consultation, which led to reactive comments. How to manage differently: Pause and label (“I’m noticing I feel boxed in”), ask one clarifying question (“What’s the priority trade-off here?”), then offer a concise alternative with estimated impact. If immediate change isn’t possible, negotiate a small area of autonomy (e.g., delivery approach). This reduces heat and creates constructive options. D. Flexible planning in a VUCA scenario (example) Situation: a release depends on an external API integration that may be delayed. Plans: Plan A (ideal): API on time — proceed with full feature set. Plan B (partial delay): Ship core features; feature-flag integration and postpone advanced features. Plan C (major delay): Reprioritize roadmap, deliver alternate value (e.g., improved docs, UX fixes). This approach creates clear triggers and reduces decision friction when uncertainty appears, keeping the team productive and adaptive. E. Small goals & measuring progress (4 weeks) Goal 1: Time-block 2 hours/week for documentation updates; track completion with calendar events and a simple checklist — target >90% completion over 4 weeks. Goal 2: Use the 60-second pause in 5 real interactions; log each instance and outcome in a short journal. Tracking: weekly review (10 minutes) of calendar/checklist + 1-page weekly reflection for behavior notes and adjustments.

radio, This practice activity is an opportunity for you to apply the concepts that you learned throughout the course. We provide a completed example activity so you can compare and contrast your work and grow as a project manager. To pass this optional activity, you must receive 100%, or 1 out of 1 point, by reviewing or completing the activity below. You can learn more about the graded and practice items in the Course Overview . Activity Overview In this activity, you will practice creating OKRs (objectives and key results) for a project. OKRs combine a goal and a metric to determine a measurable outcome. Objectives define what needs to be achieved and describe a desired outcome, while key results define how you will measure that outcome. As a project manager, creating OKRs can help you clarify both your overall project goals and the deliverables you'll need to accomplish those goals. You can also create project-level OKRs to help motivate your team. When you finish the activity, we'll take you through an exemplar of the completed assignment that you can compare to your own work. You will not be able to access the exemplar until you have completed this activity.Be sure to review these exemplars carefully, so you know what you did well and how you can improve next time. Keep in mind that some activities can have more than one right answer, just like real problems can have more than one solution. The exemplars for these activities explain one way of doing things, but they also point out where you could do things differently. This helps you check your approach to an assignment, not just your answers Scenario Review the scenario below. Then complete the step-by-step instructions. Wonder City is a mid-sized city where increasing growth and traffic are impacting quality of life. According to a recent market assessment, the region's population is expected to double in the next five years. Job growth is also expected to increase by 48%. This growth will impact street networks, parking and mobility. Wonder City has several city-wide objectives related to reducing traffic congestion and improving the city's infrastructure. In order to support these city-wide objectives, the Wonder City Transportation Authority (WCTA) will be launching five new bus lines. This initiative has been nicknamed Project Move It. You have been hired as the project manager for this initiative. As the project manager, you will set OKRs to help clarify the project goals and define what needs to be done in order to deliver a successful project. Here is some additional information about the project: The project needs to be completed within two years. Community member buy-in and support for the locations of the new bus lines will be required. The project must adhere to all government regulations. Stops along the new bus lines must connect neighboring suburbs to downtown and public resource facilities. Bus lines must service at least 50% of the most densely-populated areas of Wonder City. The project is intended to help improve wait times and increase ridership. The plan includes a marketing campaign to promote the new lines. Step-By-Step Instructions Step 1: Access the template To use the template for this course item, click the link below and select "Use Template." Link to template: Project Move It OKRs OR If you don't have a Google account, download the template directly from the attachment below. Activity Template_ Project Move It OKRs DOCX File Step 2: Draft your first objective A list of objectives for Project Move It have been provided for you below. Select one and add it next to "O1" on the first line of the OKR card. Potential objectives for Project Move It: Actively and meaningfully engage the public to generate buy-in and project support. Make it easy to get around the greater Wonder City area via public transportation. Promote public transportation as a convenient alternative to driving. Provide a reliable and consistent public transportation service. Or, if you prefer, you may draft your own objective based on the scenario. You can even try prompting a generative AI tool to help you brainstorm an objective. Remember that effective objectives are: Aspirational: Is the objective challenging and inspiring? Aligned with company goals: Does the objective support company and/or departmental OKRs? Action-oriented: Does the objective motivate the team to take initiative? Concrete: Can the project team easily grasp the objective? Significant: Will achieving the objective make a meaningful impact or change from where you are currently? For example, if the objective of an educational technology company was to provide products that consistently meet new educational standards, a project objective might be: "Successfully launch version 2.0 of our early learning app in time for the national curriculum conference." Step 3: Add key results Next, write at least three key results for your objective next to "KR1," "KR2," and "KR3." (You may add up to five key results for each objective, but only three are required for this activity.) Each key result should address the following questions: Does the key result help define success for your team? Can it be measured to prove that you've achieved your objective? Is it specific and time-bound? Is it ambitious yet realistic? Your key results should build on the scenario and additional project information, but it's up to you to determine your success criteria. As an example, let's return to the objective, "Successfully launch version 2.0 of our early learning app." If you knew that a successful launch meant getting new users to download the app, you could create any of the following key results for the objective: 15,000 new downloads within first quarter post launch 75,000 new downloads within first year post launch 25% of monthly downloads from new customers Remember: OKRs are never set in stone--they can and should be revised as you make progress, so it's okay if you need to adjust your key results later on. Step 4: Write 1-3 more OKRs Repeat steps 2 and 3 for a second, third and fourth objective to fill up the template. Pro Tip: Save the template Finally, be sure to save a blank copy of the OKR template you used to complete this activity. You can use it for further practice or in your own personal or professional projects. These templates will be useful as you put together a portfolio of project management artifacts. You can use them to work through your thought processes as you demonstrate your experience to potential employers. radio, To pass this practice quiz, you must receive 100%, or 1 out of 1 point, by completing the activity below. You can learn more about the graded and practice items in the Course Overview . Note: This is a practice activity and does not require submission. Answering the questions at the end of the activity is all that is required to complete this activity. Activity Overview In this activity you will complete a stakeholder analysis and power grid. As a project manager, it's important to understand how each stakeholder relates to your project. Completing a stakeholder analysis and power grid allows you to determine each stakeholder's influence and potential impact on a project, which is crucial to managing communications and expectations. Be sure to complete this activity before moving on. The next course item will provide you with a completed exemplar to compare to your own work. You will not be able to access the exemplar until you have completed this activity. Scenario Review the scenario below. Then complete the step-by-step instructions. You are the project manager at Office Green, a commercial landscaping company that specializes in plants and greenery for offices and other businesses. The company is getting ready to introduce its new Plant Pals service, and you will manage the launch. You and your team need to maintain trust and generate buy-in from your stakeholders. Some of your stakeholders include: Director of Product: The Director of Product is the project sponsor. As the sponsor, they fully support the project, sign off on high-level decisions, and sometimes act as a resource for the team. They are deeply invested in the outcome of the project, but less involved with its day-to-day operations. Landscape Designer/Web Designer: This person has two roles at Office Green, and within the Plant Pals project. In addition to their web design skills and knowledge of plants, they have strong relationships with a range of people across the company. The Plant Pals project could affect their role as Landscape Designer if it results in a pivot toward new services. If they don't want their role to change, it could be harder to get their buy-in. Existing clients and their employees: The core customers for this product launch are Office Green's existing clients and their employees. Their feedback can help Office Green improve the customer experience for the new service. Depending on their needs, some clients will be very interested in Plant Pals, while others will be less so. Lower-interest clients are unlikely to resist the project unless it impacts the existing product line. Office Green's investors: The investors support Office Green financially, so the company wants to keep them happy. Likewise, because Office Green's performance affects their investments, the investors want Plant Pals to succeed. However, they will not be directly involved in the project and it will not affect them before launch. They are therefore unlikely to oppose the project at this stage. Office Green's receptionist: The receptionist will not be directly involved with the Plant Pals project. They will need to answer customer questions about the service later on, but don't need to know many details until closer to launch. They have no major concerns about the project at this stage. Step-By-Step Instructions Part 1 - Understanding stakeholders with a stakeholder analysis Step 1: Access the template To use the template for this course item, click the link below and select "Use Template." Link to template: Stakeholder analysis and power grid OR If you don't have a Google account, you can download the template directly from the attachment below. Activity Template_ Stakeholder analysis and power grid PPTX File Step 2: Identify stakeholders Start with the Understanding Stakeholders table on the first slide of the template. This is where you will organize your information. First, identify the stakeholders from the Office Green scenario (e.g., Director of Product, Landscape Designer/Web Designer, etc.) and write their titles in the Stakeholder column of the table. Step 3: Determine stakeholder roles What roles do your stakeholders play in the project? Write down each team member's role in the Role column. Select from the following options when determining project roles: Project sponsor Project team member Office Green employee Office Green customer Secondary stakeholder Step 4: Determine stakeholder involvement How will each stakeholder participate in the project? What resources do they have that can help project success? Consider each stakeholder's involvement in the project, as well as any tools (software, hardware, etc.), knowledge, or relationships that could be helpful. Make note of these activities and assets in the Involvement column. Step 5: Determine the impact on your stakeholders How will the project outcomes affect the needs of each stakeholder? Do you expect any resistance that could affect their buy-in? Record this information in the Impact column. Step 6: Determine each stakeholder's level of power or influence How much influence does each stakeholder have over the project? Consider the information you added to the Involvement and Impact columns. Then record each stakeholder's level of power or influence as high (H), medium (M), or low (L) in the Power or Influence column. Note: You should gauge each stakeholder's level of influence on this project, not within Office Green in general. Step 7: Determine each stakeholder's level of interest How involved is each stakeholder in the project on a daily basis? How much will the project impact the needs of each stakeholder? Estimate each stakeholder's level of interest in the project at this stage, considering your notes from the Involvement and Impact columns. Then indicate high (H), medium (M), or low (L) in the Interest column. Be sure to consider interest in project outcomes and interest in day-to-day operations. If a stakeholder is interested in both, their overall interest level is likely high. If neither, their interest could be low. If they are interested in one, but not the other, a medium rating might be appropriate. Leave the Engagement column blank for now. You will return to it once you have completed the power grid. Part 2 - Prioritizing stakeholders in a power grid Step 1: Place stakeholders in the power grid Now go to the second slide of the template: Prioritizing Stakeholders (power grid). Consider your power or influence ratings from the stakeholder analysis. Then drag the box containing each stakeholder's name to the appropriate place in the power grid. High-interest, high-power stakeholders should go toward the upper-right corner. Low-interest, low-power stakeholders go toward the lower-left corner, and so forth. You can place stakeholders anywhere on the power grid-even between quadrants. For example, a stakeholder with a medium level of interest would straddle the high and low interest quadrants. Note: Consult slides 3-5 for a demonstration of how to place your stakeholders. Step 2: Determine how to engage with stakeholders Now that you've placed your stakeholders in the grid, go back to the Engagement column in the stakeholder analysis table. Think about where each stakeholder falls in the grid: monitor, show consideration, keep satisfied, or manage closely. Based on this information, determine how often you should communicate with each stakeholder and what form that communication should take (e.g. semi-regular consultations, frequent updates, etc.). Depending on their role or resources, you might communicate with them daily, regularly, or rarely. Record your answers in the Engagement column. Pro Tip: Add the template to your resume Finally, be sure to save a blank copy of the template you used to complete this activity. These templates are valuable records of your gained experience, ready for potential employers. Use these to build your portfolio and demonstrate hands-on skills. To highlight this on your resume, you could add: "Experienced in developing key project management documentation to support all phases of the project lifecycle." The table lists each stakeholder's level of interest as low, medium, or high. Be sure to address the following criteria in your completed power grid: The grid contains all the stakeholders from your stakeholder analysis. The position of each stakeholder corresponds to their level of interest and influence in your stakeholder analysis. In this activity, you will use that diagram to complete a WBS spreadsheet.You will use this spreadsheet to assign tasks owners and sort milestones and tasks into sequential order. Be sure to complete this activity before moving on. The next course item will provide you with a completed exemplar to compare to your own work. You will not be able to access the exemplar until you have completed this activity. Scenario Review the scenario below. Then complete the step-by-step instructions. As a project manager for Office Green, you are developing an Operations and Training plan for the new Plant Pals service. It will take six months to fully implement all protocols, including setting up operational tools, putting delivery processes in place, and training employees. You have already added milestones and tasks for this project to a WBS brainstorm diagram. Here are the milestones and their associated tasks: Establish a plant delivery and logistics plan: Team members will need to source materials for packaging and hire delivery drivers. They are also responsible for calculating the delivery fees. Select and install supply chain software and equipment: Team members will supervise vendor setup of inventory management and fulfillment software. They must also supervise vendor installation of fulfillment equipment and determine internal safety protocols for the equipment. Develop and launch an employee training program: Team members will need to develop training sessions, train employees to use the software and equipment, and monitor employee progress and improve training processes. Now you will add those tasks and milestones to a WBS spreadsheet. You will also use the sheet to record task owners and any notes about the tasks and their owners. The project sponsor for the Operations and Training plan, the Director of Operations, has put together a team for the operations launch. You can select task owners from among the following team: A Financial Analyst, who tracks and calculates costs and revenue A Fulfillment Director, who sources materials, ensures equipment is functional, and confirms fulfillment processes are correctly implemented An Inventory Manager, who maintains inventory and oversees software installation A Human Resources Specialist, who manages hiring and develops training protocols (with the help of the Training Manager) A Training Manager, who reports to the HR Specialist, runs the training program on the established protocols, and refines training processes A Quality Assurance Tester, who ensures product quality and determines safety protocols and best practices Step-by-step Instructions Step 1: Access the template To use the template for this course item, click the link below and select "Use Template." Link to template: WBS Spreadsheet OR If you don't have a Google account, you can download the template directly from the attachment below. Activity Template_ WBS Spreadsheet XLSX File Step 2: Add milestones First, open your WBS brainstorm diagram. Then record the three milestones from your brainstorm diagram under the Milestone column of your WBS Spreadsheet. Step 3: Add tasks Enter the tasks from your brainstorm diagram under the Task column of your spreadsheet. Write each task next to the corresponding milestone and task ID number. Assigning each task to an ID number helps you organize, analyze, and search for particular tasks as the list grows. Task IDs are especially useful for large or complex projects. Task ID numbers tell you two things: 1) which milestone each task relates to and 2) the sequence of the tasks. So, task 1.1 is the ID for the first task of the first milestone. Task 1.2 is the second task of the first milestone, and so on. When you finish, you should have nine tasks in your spreadsheet-three for each milestone. Step 4: Add task owners and notes To the right of the Task column are columns for Owner and Notes. Here, you can record important details that didn't fit into your WBS diagram. First, review the scenario and determine which of your team members should own each task. Then enter that person's role next to the task in the Owner column. Record any helpful details from the scenario in the Notes column. For example, including the description of the task owner's role would remind you of each person's responsibilities. If you'd like, you can also add your best estimate of how long each task might take in the Duration column (this is optional). Step 5 (Optional): Add tasks to Asana Many organizations use work management tools like Asana in addition to standard spreadsheets. Hiring managers might even ask you about your experience with work management software in interviews. That's why we recommend recreating your WBS in Asana. First, create an Asana account (if you don't already have one). Then, create a project within Asana. Finally, add milestones for each assignment and add tasks to the milestones. For more detailed instructions on how to create an account, project, or milestone, click the links below: Create an account Create a project Create a milestone (a premium Asana feature) You can also import task data into Asana using a .CSV file. Click the links below to learn more about the CSV importer. CSV importer - Asana Tips to organize your data in a spreadsheet for uploading Steps to import a spreadsheet into Asana Pro Tip: Add the template to your resume Finally, be sure to save a blank copy of the template you used to complete this activity. These templates are valuable records of your gained experience, ready for potential employers. Use these to build your portfolio and demonstrate hands-on skills. To highlight this on your resume, you could add: "Experienced in developing key project management documentation to support all phases of the project lifecycle."
